title: etcd Backup & Restore
intro: Every object in the cluster — every pod spec, every secret — lives in etcd. If etcd is gone and unrecoverable, so is your cluster. This is the single most tested disaster-recovery skill on the CKA exam.

steps.prompt: Take a snapshot backup of etcd to /tmp/etcd-backup.db.
steps.explanation: This isn't kubectl — etcdctl talks to etcd directly, which is why it needs its own TLS cert/key/CA rather than your kubeconfig.
steps.why: The three cert flags are non-negotiable on a kubeadm cluster — etcd only accepts mutually-authenticated TLS connections, even from localhost, so a plain 'etcdctl snapshot save' with no certs will just fail to connect.

steps.prompt: Verify the snapshot is valid before you trust it.
steps.explanation: This shows the snapshot's hash, revision, key count, and size — an empty or truncated snapshot would show obviously wrong numbers here.
steps.why: Checking status right after taking a backup is the only way to catch a silently corrupted or partial snapshot before you actually need it during a real disaster — by then it's too late to notice.

steps.prompt: Restore that snapshot into a new data directory.
steps.explanation: Restore always creates a NEW data directory rather than overwriting the live one — you point etcd's static pod manifest at this new directory only after confirming the restore succeeded.
steps.why: Restoring in place onto the live data directory risks corrupting a cluster that might still be partially working — restoring to a fresh directory first, then switching over, is what makes this reversible if the restore itself goes wrong.

steps.prompt: Update etcd's static pod manifest to use the restored data directory, then confirm etcd's pod is running.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
etcd-master                1/1     Running   0          20s
kube-apiserver-master      1/1     Running   0          20s
steps.explanation: Once you edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml and change --data-dir, kubelet automatically notices the change and restarts the static pod — no 'kubectl apply' needed for static pods.
steps.why: Static pods are managed by kubelet reading files directly off disk, not by the API server — that's exactly why control-plane components like etcd and kube-apiserver can run even when the API server itself is down or being restored.
